name: WHO report: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health
title: WHO report: Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health
answer: This is a World Health Organization publication, Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health. It reports that AI holds promise for diagnosis, treatment, health research, drug development and public health functions such as surveillance and outbreak response, but it must put ethics and human rights at the heart of design, deployment and use. Its most useful contribution is six consensus principles intended to ensure AI works to the public benefit of all countries, plus recommendations for governance and accountability.

sections.body: The World Health Organization publishes this report, Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health. It is a guidance document produced after eighteen months of deliberation among leading experts in ethics, digital technology, law, human rights, and experts from Ministries of Health. Its scope is the ethical challenges and risks of artificial intelligence in health, six consensus principles, and recommendations for governance. The source text does not state a publication date.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The report identifies the ethical challenges and risks with the use of artificial intelligence in health. It sets out six consensus principles intended to ensure AI works to the public benefit of all countries. It also contains recommendations intended to ensure the governance of artificial intelligence for health maximizes the promise of the technology. The source says new technologies that use artificial intelligence hold great promise to improve diagnosis, treatment, health research and drug development. It also says they can support governments carrying out public health functions, including surveillance and outbreak response. According to the report, such technologies must put ethics and human rights at the heart of their design, deployment and use. The recommendations are meant to hold all stakeholders, in the public and private sector, accountable and responsive to the healthcare workers who will rely on these technologies and to the communities and individuals whose health will be affected by their use. The guidance is described as the product of eighteen months of deliberation among leading experts in ethics, digital technology, law, human rights, and experts from Ministries of Health.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that the guidance is the product of eighteen months of deliberation. It states that the report identifies six consensus principles to ensure AI works to the public benefit of all countries. It also states that the report contains a set of recommendations for governance. No other figures, definitions or numerical claims appear in the supplied text.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in healthcare would use this source as a statement of the governance frame from the World Health Organization. It names ethics and human rights as central to design, deployment and use, and it connects AI governance to public benefit across all countries. It is useful for understanding the positions that member-state health systems may draw on when they consider AI for diagnosis, treatment, research, drug development, surveillance and outbreak response. It also points to accountability for public and private stakeholders and responsiveness to healthcare workers and affected communities.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Healthcare

sections.body: The supplied text is a short summary of the publication, not the full report. It does not state a publication date, country-specific rules, implementation steps, or detailed evidence behind the principles and recommendations. It does not give examples of AI systems or clinical results. The text is published by the World Health Organization and is institutional rather than commercial, but it is partial because it only lists the report's purpose and contents. It also repeats one sentence, which suggests the harvested text is incomplete.
